title: The Secondary Market and Equity Trading

brief.md:
- The **Securities Exchange Act of 1934** regulates the **secondary market** (investor-to-investor trading), its participants and the **registration** of broker-dealers and their representatives. The ’33 Act = primary/new-issue market.
- **All** US exchanges and OTC markets, plus broker-dealers and reps, fall under **SEC oversight**.
- **Anti-fraud provisions**: no act, practice or course of business to defraud or deceive any investor. Banned: **untrue statements of material fact**, **omissions** and **misrepresentations** of material facts. Shorthand: do not lie, cheat or steal.
- **Material information** = information that would make a difference to an investor’s decision. **Intentionally withholding** a material fact is as bad as misstating it.
- **Price manipulation** (direct or indirect) is forbidden for **registered and exempt** securities alike.
- Injured investors may **sue for damages and costs**. **Statute of limitations**: within **3 years** of the manipulative act **and** within **1 year** of discovery.
- **Common stock** is the most widely held equity security, so it is the most heavily policed by the ’34 Act in the secondary market.
> **Exam tip** ’33 Act = primary market. ’34 Act = secondary market, anti-fraud, BD/rep registration. The “which law prohibits manipulative and deceptive practices” answer is the **anti-fraud provisions**.

brief.h: Broker vs dealer, and fair pricing
brief.md:
| | **Dealer (principal)** | **Broker (agent)** |
|---|---|---|
| Role | Trades **against** the customer from its own account (**position trading**) | **Matches** a willing buyer and seller |
| Owns the security? | **Yes**, buys for or sells from **inventory** | **No**, never owns it |
| Compensation | **Mark-up** (firm sells) / **mark-down** (firm buys) | **Commission** |
| Commission charged? | **No**, the mark-up/down is the entire fee | Yes, from **each** side (buyer and seller) |
| Needs | Capital and inventory (adds liquidity) | Two counterparties on the same terms at the same time |

- Dealer example: MSFT is $100. Firm sells to client from inventory at $101 (mark-up). Client selling gets $99 (mark-down). Customer pays no commission.
- Agent example: firm matches Joe (buyer) and Jane (seller) of IBM and bills **each** a commission.
- **Hidden profits**: a firm **cannot be broker and dealer in the same transaction**. Charging both a commission and a mark-up/down on one trade is a violation. Only in an agency cross may it charge **two commissions** (one to each customer).
- **Fair prices and reasonable commissions** (MSRB G-30, FINRA Rule 2120). Factors: type of security; the firm’s right to a profit (**principal trades only**); availability of the security (easy-to-find = lower charge); dollar size (bigger order = some consideration); services rendered; expense of filling the order.
- **FINRA 5% policy**: guideline for the **maximum** mark-up/mark-down/commission. It is a **guide, not a hard rule**; more than 5% can be justified (very risky trade, illiquid security, costly order to fill). The MSRB sets no specific percentage.
- The firm’s entitlement to a profit is **not** a factor in setting an **agency commission**.
> **Exam tip** “Mark-up or mark-down” = **dealer/principal**. “Commission” = **broker/agent**. Both on the same trade = violation.

brief.h: Market makers, Nasdaq and the inside market
brief.md:
- A **market maker** is a broker-dealer that agreed to **make a market** in a stock: ready to buy **and** sell at its quoted prices during **normal market hours (9:30 am – 4:00 pm)**. It gets certain benefits and takes on obligations.
- **Nasdaq**: first electronic exchange, **second largest** in the world, **no central trading location**, all trading electronic, **many market makers per stock**. A **negotiated** marketplace: market makers must post quotes.
- **Bid** = price a market maker will **pay** (customer sells at the bid). **Ask/offer** = price it will **sell** at (customer buys at the ask). **Spread** = ask − bid.
- Quotes are **firm** and **two-sided**: must buy and sell **continuously** in regular hours, minimum **1 round lot = 100 shares** (or multiples). The bid and ask sizes may differ. After each execution the market maker must **refresh** its quote (price and size).
- Sizes are quoted in round lots: **4 × 8** = buy 400 / sell 800.
- **Backing away** (FINRA Rule 5220) = failing to honor a firm quote. **Serious violation.**
- Market makers may **not discuss or collude on pricing**; that is manipulation under the ’34 Act.

| Firm | Bid | Ask | Size |
|---|---|---|---|
| MM A | 9.92 | 9.99 | 4 × 8 |
| MM B | 9.89 | 9.96 | 12 × 3 |
| MM C | 9.90 | 10.04 | 1 × 5 |

- **Inside market** = **best (highest) bid** + **best (lowest) ask** across all market makers: here **9.92 – 9.96, size 4 × 3**. Sellers hit MM A at 9.92; buyers lift MM B at 9.96. Inside spread = 4 cents (individual spreads: 7, 7 and 14 cents).
> **Exam tip** Customer buying “at the market” pays the **lowest ask**; customer selling gets the **highest bid**. The inside spread is never wider than any single market maker’s spread.

brief.h: NYSE and stock exchanges in general
brief.md:
- Exchange purpose: provide a venue where securities are easily bought and sold; offer issuers and investors **liquidity**; the book also says exchanges act as clearinghouses (guarantee payment to the seller, deliver shares to the buyer) and automatically **report transaction data**.
- Issuers **choose** where to list. Two main national exchanges: **NYSE** and **Nasdaq**.
- Exchanges publish **initial and ongoing listing requirements** (e.g., minimum **stock price, number of shareholders, total assets**). They may **deny listing** or **expel** a listed company that fails them.
- A company that thinks its stock is undervalued may **repurchase shares in the open market**.
- **NYSE**: world’s **largest** exchange. **Auction market**: the price is the highest amount any buyer will pay meeting the lowest price any seller will take. **Dual method**: physical trading on the floor **plus** simultaneous electronic trading of the same securities.
- **Designated Market Makers (DMMs)**, formerly **specialists**: human, on the floor, **exactly one DMM per NYSE-listed security**. They keep a **fair and orderly market**, review floor and electronic data, provide accurate liquidity and pricing data, and matter most at the **open, the close and volatile periods**.

| | **NYSE** | **Nasdaq** |
|---|---|---|
| Size | Largest | Second largest |
| Venue | Floor + electronic | Fully electronic, no central location |
| Market makers | **1 DMM** per stock | **Many** per stock, no DMM |
| Pricing style | Auction | Negotiated, competing quotes |

> **Exam tip** “Which statement about NYSE and Nasdaq is accurate?” The answer: NYSE has DMMs (one per stock), Nasdaq does not.

brief.h: OTC securities: OTCBB and OTC Pink
brief.md:
- **OTC (unlisted) securities** do not trade on a national exchange. Issuers may still register shares under the ’33 Act and sell to the public. Penny stocks are a typical example.
- OTC equities are **less liquid**, **no central venue**, so **wider bid–ask spreads** (a sign of higher volatility).
- Quotes are displayed on quotation venues; they show quotes of market makers who stand ready to trade.

| | **OTC Bulletin Board (OTCBB)** | **OTC Markets / OTC Pink (Pink Sheets)** |
|---|---|---|
| Operator | **FINRA** quotation service | Second electronic quotation system |
| Shows | Real-time quotes, last sale, volume | Quotes for OTC securities |
| Listing criteria | None (no minimum price or shareholders) | **None** |
| SEC reports | **Required**: ’33 registration + ’34 reporting (10-K, 10-Q) | **Not required** (no periodic or audited reports) |
| Typical issuers | Regional and foreign equities, warrants, ADRs, DPPs | Closely held, very small, thinly traded firms |
| Quote sides | Not stated in the book | **May be one-sided** |

- To be quoted on the OTCBB (and OTC Markets) there must be **at least one market maker** willing to quote. No market maker = no quote.
- If a market maker quotes the same security on **several OTC venues**, the prices must be **identical** (FINRA Rule 6438).
- The book says FINRA is **closing the OTCBB at the end of 2021**, but it remains testable.
> **Exam tip** OTC Pink is where you should warn the client: thinly traded, little reliable information, no periodic SEC reports. Exchange quotes (NYSE, Nasdaq, BATS) must be **two-sided**; OTC Pink quotes can be one-sided.

| Market | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Third market** | **Exchange-listed securities traded OTC** (i.e., away from their primary listing venue, through an OTC market maker) |
| **Fourth market** | **ECNs**: passive computer systems that act as agents and automatically match orders, mainly **institution-to-institution** or BD members |

- **Third market** example: a BD does not route a customer’s NYSE-stock order to the NYSE but to another BD that makes a market and fills from inventory. Customer must get a price **as good as or better** than the exchange, otherwise it is a **best-execution violation**. The purpose is **best execution**, never to earn a mark-up.
- **ECNs**: accept orders **only from subscribers** (broker-dealers, large institutions), execute automatically when orders match, can run **24 hours a day, 7 days a week**, and may cost less because there is minimal human interaction.
- Institutions may clear through a **DVP/RVP** account (delivery versus payment / receipt versus payment). These accounts **do not hold securities positions**.
> **Exam tip** Third = listed stock traded OTC. Fourth = ECN / direct institution-to-institution networks. Being in the third market is neither good nor bad; it only describes where the stock traded.

brief.h: Order tickets, market and limit orders
brief.md:
- Order types by side: **buy**, **sell**, **sell short** (a sale by someone who does not own the shares).
- **Order ticket / memorandum** captures: type (buy/sell/short); terms and conditions (market, limit, stop); **account number**; **how the order was received**; **solicited, unsolicited or discretionary**; **time received** and **time entered** for execution. The customer is identified by account number, not name. Purpose: let the firm and regulators review order handling.
- **Market order**: execute **immediately** at the best available price (bid for a sale, ask for a purchase). **Guarantees execution, not price.** Has **priority over all other order types**. Best for small trades in liquid stocks; poor for large trades or illiquid securities.
- **Limit order**: a specific price **or better** (buy: at or **below**; sell: at or **above**). **Guarantees price, not execution.** May be **partially filled**. Filled at the **first price that satisfies the limit**.
- Plain language counts: “buy 100 at $25” **is** a limit order, even if the client never says “limit”. The **rep** must map the instruction to the right order type.
- Buy limits are entered **below** the current market, sell limits **above** it.
- Example: buy limit $50.63 against prints 50.65, 50.68, 50.66, 50.64, 50.62 … fills at **$50.62** (first print at or below 50.63). A buy limit at $50.40 never fills if no print is that low.
- **Day order**: valid for the trading day of entry, then cancelled. **GTC** (good ’til cancelled): stays until executed or cancelled. Most orders default to day.
- **Market-on-close**: held and executed near the end of the day as close to the closing price as possible.
> **Exam tip** Market = certainty of execution. Limit = certainty of price. Quick execution after a rumor: **market order**.

- A **stop (stop-loss) order** is a **two-step** order: (1) entered with a **stop price** that is the trigger; (2) when the market trades **at or through** the stop price, it becomes a **market order** and executes at the best available price.
- The fill can be **better or worse** than the stop price (**gap risk**). Example: buy stop at $110, best offer is $111 when triggered: fill at **$111**.
- Once triggered, stop orders are **fully executed** (the book contrasts this with limit orders, which can be partly filled).
- Use: **protect profit or prevent loss**.

| Position | Order to protect it | Triggers when price… |
|---|---|---|
| **Long** stock | **Sell stop** | falls to the stop |
| **Short** stock | **Buy stop** | rises to the stop |

- Long example: bought Intel at $27, now $31. **Sell stop $29** locks in roughly $2 of profit (depends on actual execution).
- Short example: sold short J&J at $105 (unlimited loss potential). **Buy stop $110** caps loss at about $5.

| Entered… | Orders | Mnemonic |
|---|---|---|
| **Above** the market | Sell limit, **buy stop** | **SLoBS** |
| **Below** the market | Buy limit, **sell stop** | **BLiSS** |

> **Exam tip** Stop price is a trigger, **not** a guaranteed price. Short position = buy stop. Long position = sell stop.

- On the **ex-dividend date** the stock’s price is reduced by the dividend amount.
- To prevent accidental triggering, orders entered **at or below the market** (**BLiSS**: buy limit, sell stop) are **automatically reduced by the dividend**. Adjustments only go **down**.
- Orders entered **above** the market (**SLoBS**: sell limit, buy stop) are **not adjusted**.
- **Do not reduce (DNR)** instruction: the limit or stop price is **not** reduced even if that causes execution.
- Example: stock at $50, buy limit $45 and sell stop $47.50, then a **$1.25** dividend: buy limit becomes **$43.75**, sell stop becomes **$46.25**.
- For regular-way trades the book says the ex-date is the **same day as the record date**.
> **Exam tip** “BLiSS is for divs.” Only buy limit and sell stop (below-market orders) are adjusted, by the **dividend amount**, unless DNR.

brief.h: Market protection I: best execution, order handling, reporting
brief.md:
- **Best execution** (FINRA Rule 5310; MSRB G-18): route each customer order to the venue giving the **most advantageous terms**. Often price, but volatility and liquidity can be considered. Duties: **reasonable diligence** to find the best market, and **prices as favorable as possible** under prevailing conditions. Applies to **agency and principal** trades; firms must regularly review their procedures. Example: $10 on the NYSE vs $10.10 on Nasdaq, buying on Nasdaq fails best execution.
- **Interpositioning**: adding another broker-dealer as principal when it gives **no benefit** to the customer (to generate extra fees) = best-execution violation.
- **Order-splitting / trade-shredding** (FINRA Rule 5290): breaking an order into small pieces **mainly to increase payments** (e.g., 1,000 shares into ten 100-share orders to charge ten commissions) is prohibited. Splitting to get **better or faster execution** is allowed.
- **Bona fide quotes** (FINRA Rule 5210; MSRB G-13): a firm may not publish or circulate quotes or transaction reports it does not believe are **legitimate**.
- **Trade reporting**: equity trades reported (price and volume) within **10 seconds** of execution. Municipal trades (MSRB G-14) to **RTRS** within **15 minutes**. The book notes an SEC-approved change (Sept. 2024) to **as soon as practicable, no later than 1 minute**, implementation expected around early 2026 (date not yet announced).
- **Payments to influence prices** (FINRA Rule 5230): no payments or things of value to any media outlet to move a security’s price. Exceptions: clearly identified **paid advertising** and **research reports**.
> **Exam tip** Splitting an order is not automatically wrong; the violation is splitting **for the primary purpose of increasing fees**.

brief.h: Market protection II: coordination, front-running, trading ahead, manipulation
brief.md:
- **Coordination / anti-intimidation** (FINRA Rule 5240): quotes must be set **independently**. No coordinating prices, quotes or trade reports between firms, persons or investors, and no directing, requesting or **threatening** another member to change a price or quote.
- **Payments for market making** (FINRA Rule 5250): a firm cannot accept **direct or indirect payment** (cash, non-cash or securities) from an **issuer, its affiliates or promoters** for quoting or making a market. Example: an issuer offering to pay a trader’s child’s tuition.
- **Front-running** (FINRA Rule 5270): a firm (or rep) with **material, nonpublic information about an imminent block trade** must not trade the security or a related security first. **Block = generally 10,000 shares or more** (or a large dollar amount). The rep’s own small order ahead of a big customer order is the classic case.
- **Trading ahead of customer orders** (FINRA Rule 5320): the firm may not trade for its own account at a price **equal to or better than** an unexecuted customer limit order unless it **immediately (within 60 seconds)** fills the customer order at the same or better price for at least the same number of shares. **Exceptions**: trader unaware of the order; **institutional** clients given written disclosure at opening or before each trade.
- **Trading ahead of research** (FINRA Rule 5280): no establishing, increasing or decreasing **inventory positions** (including derivatives such as calls) ahead of a research report’s publication. Needs **information barriers/firewalls** between research and trading. Concerns the firm’s **own inventory**; if the firm has advance research information, customer orders must go **agency, not principal**.
- **Other manipulation**: **marking the open/close** (orders just before the open or close to move the benchmark price); **spoofing** (orders with no intent to execute to lure others, then trade against them); **pump and dump** (hype or misleading info, often by unsolicited email or social media, to sell at a higher price; common in penny stocks); **circulating rumors** (false or misleading statements).
- **Arbitrage is not manipulation**: exploiting a temporary price gap, e.g., buy on one exchange and immediately resell higher on another.
> **Exam tip** Front-running = knowledge of a **customer’s block order**. Trading ahead of research = knowledge of a **research report**, firm inventory. Trading ahead of customer = firm’s own order ahead of a **customer’s limit order**.

traps: **Mark-up vs commission.** Dealer (principal) trades earn a **mark-up/mark-down** and carry **no commission**. Broker (agent) trades earn a **commission**. A firm can never be both broker and dealer on the same trade.

**Two commissions.** Charging a mark-up plus a commission is a hidden-profit violation. The only time two commissions arise is an agency trade where the firm matches two customers and charges **each** one.
**5% policy is a guideline.** It is a non-binding cap guide, not a hard rule. A risky trade, illiquid security or hard-to-fill order can justify more. The MSRB gives no percentage at all.
**Profit entitlement and commissions.** The firm’s right to a profit is a pricing factor on **principal** trades, **not** on agency commissions.
**Bid vs ask from the customer’s side.** Customer **sells at the bid** and **buys at the ask**. The market maker buys at the bid and sells at the ask.
**Inside market vs a single quote.** Inside market = **highest bid + lowest ask** from different market makers, so it can combine two firms. Inside spread ≤ any individual spread.
**DMMs vs market makers.** NYSE: **one** human DMM per stock (floor + electronic). Nasdaq: **no DMM**, **many** competing market makers, fully electronic. Do not say Nasdaq has DMMs for some stocks.

**OTCBB vs OTC Pink.** OTCBB issuers must be ’33-registered and file ’34 reports (10-K, 10-Q). OTC Pink has **no** reporting requirement. Neither has listing standards, and both need at least one market maker.
**Third vs fourth market.** Third = **listed** securities traded OTC through a market maker. Fourth = **ECNs**, passive computer networks matching institutional/BD orders directly.
**Limit vs stop.** Limit = guaranteed price, not execution (fills at first price meeting the limit). Stop = a trigger that turns into a **market order**; no price guarantee, possible gap risk.
**Which stop protects which position.** **Long** stock = **sell** stop (below market). **Short** stock = **buy** stop (above market). Swapping them is the classic miss.

**BLiSS vs SLoBS and dividends.** Only orders **below** the market (buy limit, sell stop) get reduced on the ex-date. Sell limit and buy stop are above the market and are **not** adjusted. DNR switches the adjustment off.

**Front-running vs trading ahead.** Front-running (5270) uses knowledge of a customer’s **block** (10,000+ shares). Trading ahead of customer orders (5320) concerns a customer **limit order** held by the firm, with a **60-second** cure. Trading ahead of research (5280) concerns a pending research report.
**Splitting orders.** Splitting is prohibited only if the **primary purpose is higher fees**. Splitting a big order to obtain better execution is fine.
**Statute of limitations.** Suit within **3 years** of the manipulation **and** **1 year** of discovery. Not 1 year only, not 3 years from discovery.

formulas.name: Inside market and spread
formulas.rule: Inside bid = HIGHEST bid of all market makers. Inside ask = LOWEST ask. Spread = ask − bid. Customer buys at the inside ask and sells at the inside bid.
formulas.example: MM1 31.40–31.46, MM2 31.42–31.50, MM3 31.38–31.45. Inside = **31.42–31.45**, spread = 31.45 − 31.42 = **3 cents** (MM1’s own spread is 6). Customer buying 100 at the market pays **$31.45**; customer selling receives **$31.42**.

formulas.name: Broker (agent) vs dealer (principal)
formulas.rule: Dealer: own inventory, counterparty, earns mark-up on sale to client / mark-down on purchase from client, no commission. Broker: matches two customers, earns commission from each, never owns the shares. Cannot be both on the same trade.
formulas.example: Stock is $40. Dealer sells to client at $40.80: mark-up **$0.80** per share, no commission. Dealer buys from client at $39.20: mark-down **$0.80**. As agent, the firm matches two clients at $40 and bills each a commission (e.g., $25 each).

formulas.name: Limit order fill logic
formulas.rule: Buy limit fills at the first print at or BELOW the limit. Sell limit fills at the first print at or ABOVE the limit. If no print qualifies, no fill. Buy limits sit below the market, sell limits above.
formulas.example: Prints: 22.10, 22.14, 22.08, 22.03, 22.12. Buy limit 22.05 fills at **22.03** (22.08 is above the limit). Sell limit 22.13 fills at **22.14** (the first print at or above 22.13). Buy limit 21.90 never fills.

formulas.name: Stop order choice and trigger
formulas.rule: Long position → SELL stop below the market. Short position → BUY stop above the market. At the stop price the order becomes a MARKET order; fill = best available price (can be worse than the stop).
formulas.example: Short 200 shares at $60 with a buy stop at $66. Stock trades at 66, best offer 66.40: order triggers and fills at **$66.40**, loss ≈ $6.40 per share, i.e., **$1,280** before costs, instead of the $6 (= $1,200) hoped for.

formulas.name: Ex-dividend adjustment (BLiSS / SLoBS)
formulas.rule: On the ex-date, reduce BELOW-market orders (buy limit, sell stop) by the cash dividend. Above-market orders (sell limit, buy stop) are unchanged. DNR = no reduction.
formulas.example: Stock $80. Buy limit $74, sell stop $76, sell limit $88, buy stop $85. Dividend **$0.60**. After ex-date: buy limit **$73.40**, sell stop **$75.40**, sell limit **$88** (unchanged), buy stop **$85** (unchanged).

formulas.name: Key numbers and deadlines
formulas.rule: Market hours 9:30 am–4:00 pm | firm quote min 1 round lot = 100 sh | block = 10,000+ sh | equity trade report 10 sec | muni trade report 15 min (RTRS) | trade-ahead cure 60 sec | 5% policy guide | lawsuit window 3 yrs from act and 1 yr from discovery | OTCBB/OTC: at least 1 market maker.
formulas.example: A BD buys 2,000 XYZ at $37 for its own account while holding an unfilled customer limit buy of 5,000 at $37: it must fill the customer within **60 seconds** at $37 or better for at least **2,000** shares.
