cards.f: Which law regulates the secondary market?
cards.b: The **Securities Exchange Act of 1934**. (The ’33 Act regulates the primary/new-issue market.)

cards.f: What does the ’34 Act require of market participants?
cards.b: **Registration**. BDs, reps, exchanges and OTC markets are all under **SEC oversight**.

cards.f: Core of the ’34 Act anti-fraud provisions
cards.b: No act, practice or course of business to **defraud or deceive** investors: no untrue statements, omissions or misrepresentations of **material facts**.

cards.f: What makes information “material”?
cards.b: It would **make a difference to an investor’s decision**.

cards.f: Is intentionally withholding a material fact a violation?
cards.b: **Yes.** Withholding is as misleading as misstating it.

cards.f: Statute of limitations for suing over price manipulation
cards.b: Within **3 years** of the act **and** within **1 year** of discovery.

cards.f: Dealer (principal) capacity: how is the firm paid?
cards.b: A **mark-up** (selling) or **mark-down** (buying). **No commission.**

cards.f: Broker (agent) capacity: how is the firm paid?
cards.b: A **commission**, charged to **each** client it matches.

cards.f: Can a firm be broker and dealer in the same transaction?
cards.b: **No.** Charging both a commission and a mark-up/down is a **hidden-profit** violation.

cards.f: Only case with two commissions on one trade
cards.b: An **agency trade matching two customers**: each pays a commission and each is owed best execution.

cards.f: Which rules require fair prices and reasonable commissions?
cards.b: **MSRB G-30** and **FINRA Rule 2120**.

cards.f: FINRA 5% policy: rule or guideline?
cards.b: A **guideline** for maximum mark-up/mark-down/commission. Firms **can** exceed it for risky, illiquid or costly orders.

cards.f: Does the MSRB set a percentage for fair pricing?
cards.b: **No.** The 5% policy is FINRA’s.

cards.f: Is the firm’s right to a profit a factor in agency commissions?
cards.b: **No.** It is a factor only for **principal** trades.

cards.f: Normal market hours for a market maker’s obligation
What is a round lot?
cards.b: **100 shares** or a multiple of 100.

cards.f: Minimum size of a market maker’s firm two-sided quote
cards.b: **One round lot (100 shares)** on each side.

cards.f: Bid vs ask
cards.b: Bid = what the market maker **pays** (customer sells). Ask/offer = what it **charges** (customer buys).

cards.f: Size notation 4 × 8 means what?
cards.b: Bid for **400** shares, offer of **800** shares (round lots).

cards.f: What is backing away?
cards.b: Failing to honor a **firm quote**. A serious violation (FINRA Rule 5220).

cards.f: Customer sells but the market maker refuses to buy at its posted bid: violation?
cards.b: **Backing away.**

cards.f: May market makers discuss how to price a stock together?
cards.b: **No.** That is collusion/manipulation under the ’34 Act.

cards.f: Inside market definition
cards.b: The **highest bid** and **lowest ask** from any market makers.

cards.f: What does a customer pay buying “at the market” on Nasdaq?
cards.b: The **lowest ask** across market makers (best execution).

cards.f: NYSE vs Nasdaq: market makers per stock
cards.b: NYSE: exactly **one DMM**. Nasdaq: **many** market makers, no DMM.

cards.f: What does a DMM do?
cards.b: Directs and supervises floor trading, maintains a **fair and orderly market**, and matters most at the **open, close and volatility**.

cards.f: How does NYSE trading work?
cards.b: An **auction** market with floor trading **plus** simultaneous electronic trading.

cards.f: What can an exchange do to a non-compliant listed company?
cards.b: **Deny initial listing or expel** it for failing price, shareholder or asset requirements.

cards.f: Why are OTC bid–ask spreads often wider?
cards.b: Less liquidity, fewer shares traded, no central venue: signals **more volatility**.

cards.f: Who operates the OTCBB?
cards.b: **FINRA**. It displays real-time quotes, last sale and volume for OTC equities.

cards.f: What can be quoted on the OTCBB?
cards.b: Regional and foreign equities, warrants, **ADRs** and **DPPs**.

cards.f: OTCBB entry requirements
cards.b: No minimum price or shareholders, but **’33 Act registration** and ’34 reports (**10-K, 10-Q**).

cards.f: Minimum number of market makers needed to be quoted on OTCBB/OTC Markets
cards.b: **One.** No market maker means no quote.

cards.f: OTC Pink: other name and origin
cards.b: **OTC Markets**, formerly the **Pink Sheets** (named for the paper quotes were printed on).

cards.f: Does OTC Pink require SEC periodic reports?
cards.b: **No.** No periodic reports or audited statements; reliable information can be hard to find.

cards.f: Same security quoted on two OTC venues by one market maker
cards.b: Prices must be **identical** (FINRA Rule 6438).

cards.f: One-sided quotes allowed where?
cards.b: **OTC Pink** can be one-sided. NYSE, Nasdaq and BATS quotes must be **two-sided**.

cards.f: Third market
cards.b: **Exchange-listed securities traded over-the-counter.**

cards.f: Why route a listed-stock order to an OTC market maker?
cards.b: To obtain **best execution**: price as good as or better than the exchange. Never to earn a mark-up.

cards.f: Fourth market
cards.b: **ECNs**: passive computer systems that match orders, mainly institutional.

cards.f: ECN operating hours and who may use them
cards.b: Up to **24/7**; only **subscribers** (BDs, large institutions).

cards.f: DVP/RVP account
cards.b: Institutional settlement account (delivery/receipt versus payment) that **holds no securities positions**.

cards.f: Which order details must the order ticket capture?
cards.b: Buy/sell/short, terms, **account number**, how received, solicited/unsolicited/discretionary, **time received and entered**.

cards.f: Market order guarantee
cards.b: **Execution** at the best available price. **Price not guaranteed.** Priority over other orders.

cards.f: Limit order guarantee
cards.b: **Price** (or better), not execution.

cards.f: Client says “buy 100 at $25” with no other words: what order is it?
cards.b: A **buy limit** at $25. The rep must interpret it.

cards.f: Where does a limit order fill?
cards.b: At the **first price that satisfies** the limit.

cards.f: Day order vs GTC
cards.b: Day: expires end of the entry day. GTC: lasts until **executed or cancelled**.

cards.f: What happens when a stop order is triggered?
cards.b: It becomes a **market order** and fills at the best available price, possibly worse than the stop (**gap risk**).

cards.f: Which stop protects a long position? A short position?
cards.b: Long: **sell stop**. Short: **buy stop**.

cards.f: Where are BLiSS and SLoBS orders entered?
cards.b: BLiSS (buy limit, sell stop): **below** the market. SLoBS (sell limit, buy stop): **above**.

cards.f: Which orders are reduced for a dividend on the ex-date?
cards.b: **BLiSS** orders, by the **dividend amount**. SLoBS are not adjusted.

cards.f: What does a DNR instruction do?
cards.b: Prevents the limit/stop price from being reduced on the ex-date, even if the order then executes.

cards.f: Best execution duties (FINRA 5310 / MSRB G-18)
cards.b: Use **reasonable diligence** to find the best market and execute at prices **as favorable as possible**; applies to agency and principal trades.

cards.f: Interpositioning
cards.b: Adding an **unnecessary extra principal BD** with no customer benefit, often for fees; a best-execution violation.

cards.f: When is order-splitting prohibited (Rule 5290)?
cards.b: When done **mainly to increase fees**. Splitting for better/faster execution is permitted.

cards.f: Time limit to report an equity trade
cards.b: **10 seconds** after execution.

cards.f: Muni trade reporting under the book’s current rule
cards.b: To RTRS within **15 minutes** (MSRB G-14); change to ≤ 1 minute approved but implementation date not announced.

cards.f: Payments to media to influence a security’s price
cards.b: Prohibited (FINRA 5230). Exceptions: identified **paid advertising** and **research reports**.

cards.f: Rule 5240 coordination
cards.b: No coordinating quotes/prices/trade reports, and no **threatening** another member to change a quote.

cards.f: Can an issuer pay a firm to make a market in its stock?
cards.b: **No** (Rule 5250). Direct or indirect payments in cash, non-cash or securities are banned.

cards.f: Front-running
cards.b: Trading on **nonpublic knowledge of an imminent block** (Rule 5270). Block ≈ **10,000+ shares**.

cards.f: Rule 5320: firm buys for itself at or better than an unfilled customer limit
cards.b: Must fill the customer **within 60 seconds** at the same or better price for at least the same shares.

cards.f: Exceptions to the trading-ahead-of-customer rule
cards.b: Trader **unaware** of the order, or **institutional** client given written disclosure.

cards.f: Rule 5280 trading ahead of research
cards.b: No position changes (incl. calls) before a report is published; keep **firewalls**; customer orders go **agency**.

cards.f: Marking the open/close
cards.b: Orders placed just before open/close to manipulate the benchmark opening or closing price.

cards.f: Spoofing
cards.b: Entering orders **with no intent to execute** to lure others, then trading against them.

cards.f: Pump and dump
cards.b: Hyping a stock (e.g., unsolicited email in a penny stock) to inflate the price and sell.

cards.f: Is arbitrage manipulation?
cards.b: **No.** It exploits a temporary price disparity, e.g., buying on one exchange and reselling higher on another.

cards.f: Exchange services beyond providing a venue
cards.b: Gives issuers and investors **liquidity**, acts as a **clearinghouse** (guarantees payment to the seller, delivers shares to the buyer) and **automatically reports** transaction data.

cards.f: Why might a company buy back its own shares in the open market?
cards.b: It believes its stock is **undervalued**.

cards.f: When is a market order the right choice?
cards.b: **Small trades in liquid stocks** where immediate execution matters more than price. Poor fit for large trades, illiquid securities or when a specific price is wanted.

cards.f: Partial fills: limit order vs triggered stop order
cards.b: A **limit** order can be **partially filled**. A triggered **stop** (now a market order) is **fully executed**.

cards.f: For regular-way trades, how do the ex-dividend date and the record date relate?
cards.b: They fall on the **same day**.

cards.f: What is position trading?
cards.b: A BD acting as **dealer/principal** trades for its **own account**, buying into or selling from **inventory**, which adds liquidity and allows near-instant execution.

cards.f: What is needed for a firm to execute a trade as agent?
cards.b: **Two market participants** (other than the BD) willing to trade on the **same terms at the same time**. The firm never buys or owns the shares.

cards.f: Which equity security is most widely held and so heavily policed by the ’34 Act?
cards.b: **Common stock.**

questions.q: The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 is primarily concerned with which of the following?
o: Registration of new issues sold to the public for the first time
Trading of securities between investors and the registration of broker-dealers and their representatives
Setting the dividend policy of listed companies
Establishing the maximum price at which an issuer may sell new shares
w: Wrong: new-issue registration belongs to the primary market, which is governed by the ’33 Act, not the ’34 Act.
Correct: the ’34 Act governs the secondary market and requires participants such as broker-dealers and their reps to be registered.
Wrong: the ’34 Act does not dictate what dividends a listed company pays to shareholders.
Wrong: pricing of new issues is not set by the ’34 Act, which concerns secondary trading and anti-fraud.

questions.q: An investor injured by price manipulation wishes to sue for damages. Under the statute of limitations, the suit must be brought:
o: within 1 year of the manipulation and within 3 years of discovery
within 1 year of the manipulation only
within 3 years of discovery only
within 3 years of the manipulation and within 1 year of discovery
w: Wrong: the numbers are swapped; 3 years runs from the manipulative act and 1 year from discovery.
Wrong: 1 year from the act is not the rule; the act-based period is 3 years, combined with 1 year from discovery.
Wrong: discovery alone does not set the outer limit; the 3-year period from the manipulative act also applies.
Correct: both clocks apply, so suit must come within 3 years of the act and within 1 year of discovery.

questions.q: A registered representative knows that a company has just lost its largest customer, a fact not yet public. When recommending the stock she describes only its strong earnings and says nothing about the lost customer. Which statement is most accurate?
o: This is a violation because intentionally omitting a material fact is as misleading as misstating one
There is no violation because the information is not yet public
There is no violation because every statement she made was true
This is a violation only if the client actually loses money
w: Correct: the anti-fraud provisions cover omissions of material facts, and deliberate withholding is as misleading as a false statement.
Wrong: non-public status does not excuse the omission; the issue is that the client lacks material information for the decision.
Wrong: true statements do not cure the problem when a material fact is deliberately left out of the discussion.
Wrong: the violation is the deceptive omission itself; a resulting loss only matters for damages, not for whether a violation occurred.

questions.q: The anti-fraud provisions of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 prohibit all of the following EXCEPT:
o: an untrue statement of a material fact
an omission of a material fact
a dealer selling a security to a customer from its own inventory at a disclosed, reasonable mark-up
a misrepresentation of a material fact
w: Wrong: untrue statements of material fact are specifically prohibited by the anti-fraud provisions.
Wrong: omitting material facts is expressly prohibited as a form of deception.
Correct: principal trades with a fair mark-up are a normal dealer activity, so this is the one item that is not prohibited.
Wrong: misrepresenting material facts is prohibited just like outright false statements.

questions.q: A customer buys 500 shares from a broker-dealer that sells them out of its own inventory. How does the firm earn its compensation on this trade?
o: A mark-down subtracted from the price
A commission charged to the customer
A mark-up added to the price
A commission charged to both the customer and an unnamed seller
w: Wrong: a mark-down applies when the dealer buys from the customer, not when it sells.
Wrong: commissions are charged by a firm acting as agent, and this firm is trading as principal from inventory.
Correct: when a dealer sells to a customer from inventory, its compensation is the mark-up built into the price.
Wrong: no second party is involved; the firm itself is the counterparty, so no matched-trade commissions apply.

questions.q: Firm Z receives an order from Customer A to buy stock and an order from Customer B to sell the same quantity at an agreeable price. It crosses the two orders. Which statement is correct?
o: Firm Z owns the stock briefly and earns a mark-up
Firm Z acts as principal and charges a mark-down to Customer B
Firm Z may charge a commission to Customer A and a mark-up to Customer B
Firm Z acts as agent, never owns the stock, and charges each customer a commission
w: Wrong: matching two customers is agency business; the firm does not take the shares into its own inventory.
Wrong: a mark-down is a principal-trade charge and the firm is not a principal here.
Wrong: using a commission on one side and a mark-up on the other mixes capacities, which is not allowed in the same transaction.
Correct: in an agency trade the firm only matches counterparties and is paid a commission by each of them.

questions.q: A dealer sells shares to a client from inventory at a price that includes a mark-up and then also bills the client a separate commission on the same trade. This conduct is:
o: acceptable if the client is told in writing beforehand
a violation, because a firm cannot be both broker and dealer in the same transaction
acceptable if the trade is for a block of 10,000 shares or more
acceptable if the combined charge is under 5%
w: Wrong: written disclosure does not turn a prohibited dual capacity into a permitted one.
Correct: a firm is either the customer’s counterparty or the matchmaker; charging both a mark-up and a commission is a hidden-profit violation.
Wrong: trade size has no bearing on the rule against acting as both broker and dealer.
Wrong: the 5% guideline concerns reasonableness of charges, but it does not allow mixing the two capacities.

questions.q:
Which of the following are permitted charges by a broker-dealer?

I. A mark-up and a commission on the same trade
II. A commission to both the buyer and the seller when matching them as agent
III. A mark-down on a principal purchase from a customer
IV. A mark-up on a principal sale to a customer
o: II, III and IV only
II only
I and II only
I, III and IV only
w: Correct: an agency match can bill each side a commission, and principal trades can carry a mark-down on purchases or a mark-up on sales.
Wrong: this is incomplete because mark-downs and mark-ups on genuine principal trades are also allowed.
Wrong: item I combines both capacities on one trade, which is a hidden-profit violation.
Wrong: this includes the prohibited mark-up plus commission combination and leaves out the permitted agency commissions.

questions.q: Under FINRA’s 5% policy as a general guide, what is the approximate maximum mark-up a dealer should charge on a principal sale of $8,000 of stock to a customer?
w: Correct: 5% × $8,000 = $400, the general guide, though it can be exceeded for justified circumstances.
Wrong: $80 is only 1% of the trade value; the policy guide is five percent.
Wrong: $800 is 10%, double what the 5% guideline suggests.
Wrong: $4,000 would be 50% of the trade, far beyond any reasonable guideline.

questions.q: Which statement about FINRA’s 5% policy is most accurate?
o: It applies only to commissions and never to mark-ups
It is a hard cap, and no mark-up or commission may ever exceed 5%
It is a guideline, and a higher charge may be justified for an illiquid or hard-to-fill order
It sets the minimum commission a broker-dealer must charge
w: Wrong: the guide covers mark-ups, mark-downs and commissions alike.
Wrong: the policy is described as a guide, not a hard-and-fast rule, so exceeding 5% is not automatically a violation.
Correct: circumstances such as a risky trade, an illiquid security or an expensive order to fill can justify more than 5%.
Wrong: it concerns the maximum reasonable amount, not a minimum charge.

questions.q: When setting fair prices and commissions, a firm must consider all of the following factors EXCEPT:
o: the type of security involved
the dollar size of the transaction
the expense of filling the order
the firm’s entitlement to a profit when it is acting as agent
w: Wrong: the type of security is one of the listed factors in judging fairness of the charge.
Wrong: dollar size matters because larger orders should receive some consideration on cost.
Wrong: the expense involved in filling the order is a recognized factor.
Correct: the firm’s right to a profit is relevant only to principal trades, not to a commission in an agency transaction.

questions.q: Which organization’s policy provides the 5% guide for mark-ups, mark-downs and commissions?
o: MSRB
FINRA
Nasdaq
The NYSE
w: Wrong: the MSRB requires fair prices but offers no specific percentage in the book.
Correct: the 5% policy is FINRA’s guide to the maximum reasonable charge.
Wrong: Nasdaq is a marketplace and does not publish the 5% pricing guide.
Wrong: the NYSE is an exchange and is not the source of the 5% policy.

questions.q: At a minimum, what must a Nasdaq market maker’s firm two-sided quote cover?
o: 50 shares on each side
There is no minimum size
200 shares to buy and 100 shares to sell
100 shares on each side
w: Wrong: 50 shares is less than a round lot, which is the minimum.
Wrong: there is a minimum, which is one round lot of 100 shares.
Wrong: 200 shares on the buy side is a size a market maker may choose to quote, but the required minimum on each side is a single round lot of 100 shares.
Correct: a firm quote must be good for at least one round lot, meaning 100 shares, on both the bid and ask.

questions.q: A market maker quotes a stock at 18.40 – 18.46. What is the bid–ask spread?
w: Correct: spread = ask − bid = 18.46 − 18.40 = $0.06, or 6 cents.
Wrong: $0.04 does not equal the ask minus the bid; the difference is larger.
Wrong: $0.46 is just the cents portion of the ask, not the difference between the two prices.
Wrong: $0.60 misplaces the decimal; the correct difference is 6 cents.

questions.q: A Nasdaq market maker displays a quote of 52.30 – 52.36. A customer’s firm sends an order to sell 200 shares to it at 52.30 during regular hours, and the market maker declines to buy. This practice is called:
o: marking the close
backing away
interpositioning
front-running
w: Wrong: marking the close involves orders entered near the close to influence the closing price, which is not what happened here.
Correct: failing to honor a firm quote is backing away, a serious violation under FINRA Rule 5220.
Wrong: interpositioning means adding an unnecessary broker-dealer to a trade, not refusing to honor a quote.
Wrong: front-running means trading ahead of an imminent block using non-public knowledge.

questions.q: Three Nasdaq market makers quote a stock: A at 24.10 – 24.18, B at 24.12 – 24.20, and C at 24.08 – 24.16. A customer enters an order to sell 100 shares at the market. How much per share does the customer receive?
w: Wrong: 24.08 is the lowest bid, which would give the seller the worst price rather than the best.
Wrong: 24.10 is only the second-best bid, so a seller would not get it with best execution.
Correct: the seller receives the highest bid; the bids are 24.10, 24.12 and 24.08, so the best is 24.12 from B.
Wrong: 24.16 is the lowest ask, the price a buyer would pay, not a seller’s proceeds.

questions.q: Market maker A quotes 40.50 – 40.55 (5 × 3). Market maker B quotes 40.52 – 40.58 (2 × 6). Market maker C quotes 40.49 – 40.54 (8 × 4). How is the inside market shown, with bid size × ask size?
w: Correct: the highest bid is 40.52 from B (size 2) and the lowest ask is 40.54 from C (size 4), giving 40.52 – 40.54, 2 × 4.
Wrong: this is only one firm’s quote and is not the combination of the best bid and best ask across firms.
Wrong: this takes the widest prices (lowest bid and highest ask), the opposite of the inside market.
Wrong: the prices are right but the sizes come from the wrong firms; the sizes must belong to the firms posting the best prices.

questions.q:
Which of the following describe a Nasdaq market maker’s quotations?

I. They are firm
II. They are two-sided
III. They may be one-sided if the stock is thinly traded
IV. They must be for at least one round lot
o: I and II only
II and III only
I, II and IV only
I, III and IV only
w: Wrong: this is incomplete because the quote must also be for at least one round lot.
Wrong: this includes the false claim that one-sided quotes are acceptable and omits the firm-quote requirement.
Correct: the quote is firm, two-sided and at least one round lot; one-sided quoting is not allowed on Nasdaq.
Wrong: item III is false for Nasdaq, since a bid and an ask must both be posted.

questions.q: Two Nasdaq market makers in the same stock agree over lunch to keep their quotes at identical prices for the rest of the week. This is:
o: acceptable, because both are registered market makers
acceptable, because the quotes remain firm
prohibited only if the stock is a penny stock
prohibited, because discussing or colluding on pricing is market manipulation
w: Wrong: being registered does not allow market makers to agree on how to price a security.
Wrong: firm quotes do not cure collusion; the problem is the agreement on prices.
Wrong: the prohibition applies to all securities, not only penny stocks.
Correct: market makers may not discuss or collude on pricing, which would violate the ’34 Act as manipulation.

questions.q: During which hours must a market maker be ready to buy and sell at its quoted prices?
o: 8:00 am to 5:00 pm
9:30 am to 4:00 pm
9:00 am to 9:00 pm
24 hours a day
w: Wrong: these hours are wider than the normal market hours the obligation covers.
Correct: the obligation applies during normal market hours of 9:30 am to 4:00 pm.
Wrong: this window runs far beyond normal market hours; the quoting obligation covers regular trading hours only, 9:30 am to 4:00 pm.
Wrong: round-the-clock operation is a feature of ECNs, not a market maker’s quoting obligation.

questions.q: How many designated market makers (DMMs) are assigned to each NYSE-listed security?
o: None, because the NYSE is fully electronic
Two, one for buying and one for selling
Exactly one
As many as wish to register
w: Wrong: the NYSE combines floor trading with electronic trading and does use human DMMs.
Wrong: a single DMM handles both sides of the market for its assigned stock.
Correct: each NYSE-listed security has exactly one DMM overseeing its trading.
Wrong: unlimited competing market makers describes Nasdaq, not the NYSE.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the NYSE and Nasdaq?
o: The NYSE has one DMM per stock, while Nasdaq has no DMMs and relies on multiple market makers
Nasdaq is the world’s largest exchange and the NYSE is the second largest
Both exchanges use designated market makers on a trading floor
Nasdaq uses a single DMM per stock and the NYSE uses several competing market makers
w: Correct: the NYSE assigns exactly one human DMM per stock, whereas Nasdaq is fully electronic with many market makers and no DMM.
Wrong: the NYSE is the largest in the world and Nasdaq is second largest.
Wrong: Nasdaq has no trading floor and no DMM-like figure.
Wrong: this reverses the two structures; the single DMM model belongs to the NYSE.

questions.q: All of the following describe the New York Stock Exchange EXCEPT:
o: it operates as an auction market
it conducts floor trading and electronic trading simultaneously
each listed security has a designated market maker
it has no central trading location and all trades occur electronically
w: Wrong: the NYSE does operate as an auction marketplace, so this is a true description.
Wrong: the NYSE runs physical floor trading and electronic trading of the same securities at once.
Wrong: every NYSE-listed security has one DMM, so this statement is accurate.
Correct: having no central location with fully electronic trading describes Nasdaq, not the NYSE, which has a physical floor.

questions.q: After listing, a company’s shareholder base and total assets fall below an exchange’s ongoing listing requirements. What authority does the exchange have?
o: None, because listing standards apply only at initial listing
It may expel the company from the exchange
It may only issue a warning letter
It must transfer the company to the NYSE
w: Wrong: exchanges publish both initial and ongoing requirements and can enforce either.
Correct: an exchange can deny an initial listing or expel an already-listed company that fails the criteria.
Wrong: the book gives the exchange the authority to expel; a warning is not the described limit of its power.
Wrong: failing standards does not entitle a company to move to another exchange automatically.

questions.q: Why are bid–ask spreads on OTC equities often much wider than those of exchange-listed stocks?
o: Because OTC securities are more liquid
Because OTC securities are exempt from the ’34 Act
Because OTC securities are traded less and have no centralized venue
Because OTC securities are quoted only by the exchange
w: Wrong: OTC equities are generally less liquid, not more, which is what widens the spread.
Wrong: OTC markets are subject to SEC oversight under the ’34 Act.
Correct: fewer shares trade and there is no central marketplace, so spreads widen, indicating higher volatility.
Wrong: OTC quotes are displayed on OTC quotation venues, not by an exchange.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the requirements for an issuer’s equity to be quoted on the OTC Bulletin Board?
o: It must meet a minimum share price and minimum number of shareholders
It must be registered under the ’33 Act and file ’34 Act reports such as 10-Ks and 10-Qs
It has no requirements at all
It must be listed on Nasdaq first
w: Wrong: the OTCBB has no minimum stock price or minimum number of shareholders, unlike national exchanges.
Correct: the basic requirement is registered shares under the ’33 Act and ongoing ’34 Act disclosure through 10-Ks and 10-Qs.
Wrong: although listing standards are absent, the issuer must still file current financial reports with the SEC.
Wrong: OTCBB securities are non-exchange securities and need no prior Nasdaq listing.

questions.q: What is the minimum number of market makers required for a security to be quoted on the OTC Bulletin Board?
o: One
Zero, since OTC securities have no market makers
Two
Three
w: Correct: at least one firm must agree to act as market maker and enter quotes.
Wrong: with no market maker there would be no quotes, so a quote cannot exist without one.
Wrong: two is not required; one willing market maker is enough.
Wrong: three is not a requirement in the chapter.

questions.q: A client wants to buy 1,000 shares of a company that trades on OTC Pink after hearing a tip. What should the representative tell the client?
o: The stock is guaranteed two-sided quotes at all times
The company must meet strict listing standards to be quoted
The company must file periodic reports with the SEC, so information is easy to find
The stock may be thinly traded and reliable information about the company may be hard to find
w: Wrong: OTC Pink quotes may be one-sided, so two-sided quotes are not guaranteed.
Wrong: OTC Pink has no formal listing requirements.
Wrong: OTC Pink companies do not have to file periodic reports or audited financials with the SEC.
Correct: many OTC Pink companies are tiny, closely held or thinly traded, with limited and unreliable public information.

questions.q:
Which of the following are true of OTC Markets (OTC Pink)?

I. It was formerly known as the Pink Sheets
II. Quoted companies must file 10-Qs with the SEC
III. Quotes may be one-sided
IV. It has no formal listing requirements
o: I and II only
I, II and IV only
II, III and IV only
I, III and IV only
w: Wrong: item II is false because OTC Pink does not require periodic SEC reports such as 10-Qs.
Wrong: item II again wrongly imposes SEC periodic reporting, which OTC Pink does not require.
Wrong: this includes the false requirement to file 10-Qs and omits the true Pink Sheets history.
Correct: it is the former Pink Sheets, quotes can be one-sided, and there are no formal listing requirements.

questions.q: A market maker posts a bid of $1.05 for Security A on OTC Pink while simultaneously posting a bid of $1.12 for Security A on another OTC venue. Which statement is correct?
o: This is permitted because each venue is a separate market
This violates the requirement that quotes for the same security on multiple OTC venues be the same
This is permitted if the market maker’s quote on each venue is at least one round lot
This is a third-market transaction
w: Wrong: separate venues do not allow different quotes from the same market maker for the same security.
Correct: FINRA Rule 6438 requires a market maker quoting the same security on multiple OTC venues to quote the same prices.
Wrong: quote size does not solve the problem; the rule is about price consistency across venues.
Wrong: the third market refers to exchange-listed securities traded OTC, which is not described here.

questions.q: A broker-dealer receives a customer’s order to buy an NYSE-listed stock and, instead of sending it to the NYSE, sends it to an OTC market maker that fills it from inventory at a price better than the NYSE quote. This is a:
o: fourth-market trade, justified by best execution
primary-market trade
third-market trade, justified by best execution
second-market trade, justified by earning a mark-up
w: Wrong: the fourth market refers to ECNs and direct institutional networks, not an OTC market maker filling from inventory.
Wrong: the primary market is where new issues are sold; this is secondary-market trading.
Correct: an exchange-listed security traded over-the-counter is a third-market trade, and routing there is acceptable to obtain best execution.
Wrong: earning a mark-up is not a valid reason for routing, and the market is not called the second market in the chapter.

questions.q: Which market is made up of passive computer systems that automatically match subscribers’ buy and sell orders?
o: Fourth market
Third market
OTC Bulletin Board
NYSE floor
w: Correct: ECNs, also called the fourth market, automatically match orders from subscribers.
Wrong: the third market is listed securities traded OTC, usually through market makers.
Wrong: the OTCBB is a FINRA quotation service displaying market makers’ quotes.
Wrong: the NYSE floor has human DMMs supervising an auction market.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of an electronic communications network (ECN)?
o: It acts as a passive agent that matches orders automatically
It can operate 24 hours per day, seven days per week
It accepts orders only from its subscribers
It buys and sells for its own account from inventory to fill orders
w: Wrong: ECNs are passive systems acting as agents, so this is a true feature.
Wrong: ECNs may operate around the clock, so this describes a real feature.
Wrong: only subscribers, such as broker-dealers and large institutions, may place orders.
Correct: trading from inventory is a dealer function; an ECN only matches orders between its members.

questions.q: Large institutions trading directly with each other on a private OTC computer network, rather than on an exchange such as the NYSE or Nasdaq, are participating in the:
o: first market
fourth market
third market
pink market
w: Wrong: the chapter does not describe this activity as a first market.
Correct: direct institutional trading on a private OTC computer network is the fourth market, typified by ECNs.
Wrong: the third market is exchange-listed securities traded OTC, usually via market makers rather than institution-to-institution networks.
Wrong: the pink market refers to OTC Pink quotations for small, thinly traded securities, not institutional ECN trading.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT recorded on a customer’s order ticket?
o: The customer’s name
The time the order was received
Whether the order was solicited
The account number
w: Correct: the ticket identifies the customer by account number, so the customer's name is the one item not captured on it.
Wrong: the time the order was received and the time it was entered for execution are both recorded.
Wrong: the ticket records whether the order was solicited, unsolicited or discretionary.
Wrong: the account number is one of the key items captured on the order ticket.

questions.q: A client hears a rumor that a company will make a major announcement within minutes and wants to buy the stock as quickly as possible. Which order should be entered?
o: Sell stop order
Buy limit order
Market order
Good ’til cancelled limit order
w: Wrong: a sell stop is used to protect a long position, not to buy a stock.
Wrong: a buy limit sits below the market and may never fill if the price rises on the news.
Correct: a market order is the type that gives immediate execution at the best available price.
Wrong: a GTC limit order stays open but guarantees only a price, not a prompt execution.

questions.q: When a customer enters a market order to buy 200 shares, the quote on the screen is 33.10 – 33.14. By the time the order reaches the market, the quote has moved to 33.12 – 33.16. What is the total cost of the purchase, ignoring fees?
w: Wrong: $6,620 uses a price of 33.10, the old bid, which is not a price a buyer pays.
Wrong: $6,624 corresponds to 33.12, the new bid, which a buyer does not pay.
Correct: a buyer pays the ask at the time of execution, 33.16 × 200 = $6,632.
Wrong: $6,628 corresponds to 33.14, the old ask; the market order executes at the current quote when it arrives.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes a limit order?
o: It guarantees execution but not price
It guarantees price but not execution
It guarantees both price and execution
It guarantees neither price nor execution
w: Wrong: guaranteed execution with no price guarantee describes a market order.
Correct: a limit order locks in the price or better, but if the price is not available the order will not execute.
Wrong: no order type guarantees both, since a limit price may never be reached.
Wrong: a limit order does guarantee the price (or better) if it is filled.

questions.q: A customer enters an order to buy 300 shares at 41.20. The following trades occur in sequence: 41.25, 41.31, 41.28, 41.22, 41.19, 41.15. At what price is the order executed?
w: Correct: a buy limit at 41.20 fills at the first print at or below 41.20; the first such print in the sequence is 41.19.
Wrong: 41.15 is a later print; the order fills at the first price that satisfies the limit.
Wrong: the order does not necessarily fill at the limit price; it fills at the first qualifying print, which here is lower.
Wrong: 41.22 is above the 41.20 limit, so the customer would not accept it.

questions.q: A customer places an order to sell 500 shares at 62.40 or better. Subsequent trades print at 62.35, 62.38, 62.41, 62.44, 62.40. What are the gross proceeds of the sale?
w: Wrong: $31,175 uses 62.35, which is below the sell limit and therefore never qualifies.
Wrong: $31,200 assumes a fill at exactly the limit of 62.40, but the first qualifying print came earlier at 62.41.
Wrong: $31,220 would require 62.44, a later print than the first qualifying one.
Correct: the sell limit fills at the first print at or above 62.40, which is 62.41; 62.41 × 500 = $31,205.

questions.q: A customer enters a limit order marked GTC. How long does the order remain in effect?
o: Until it is executed or cancelled
Until the next ex-dividend date
For exactly 30 days
Until the end of the trading day
w: Correct: good ’til cancelled means the order stays in force until it is filled or the customer cancels it.
Wrong: the ex-dividend date can adjust the price of certain orders but does not end a GTC order.
Wrong: no fixed 30-day period is part of the GTC definition in this chapter.
Wrong: lasting only through the trading day describes a day order, the default for most orders.

questions.q: A stock trades at $23. A client tells her representative: “Sell 100 shares at $25.” What type of order is this, and what will happen?
o: A market order that executes immediately at $23
A sell limit entered above the market that fills only if the stock trades at $25 or higher
A sell stop entered above the market that triggers at $25
A buy limit that fills at the first price below $25
w: Wrong: naming a specific price turns the instruction into a limit order, not a market order.
Correct: a stated price means a limit order; as a sell limit above the current market it waits until $25 or better is available.
Wrong: a sell stop is entered below the market and becomes a market order when triggered, which is not the instruction given.
Wrong: the client wants to sell, so this is a sell order rather than a buy limit.

questions.q: What is a market-on-close order?
o: An order executed immediately at the opening price
A stop order that triggers at the close
An order held and executed near the end of trading as close to the closing price as possible
An order that is cancelled if not filled by the close
w: Wrong: execution at the open is the opposite timing of what market-on-close describes.
Wrong: a market-on-close order does not wait for a stop price to trigger.
Correct: the order is held until late in the session and executed as close to the closing price as possible.
Wrong: cancellation at the end of the day describes the fate of an unfilled day order.

questions.q: What happens when the market price reaches the stop price of a stop order?
o: The order executes only at exactly the stop price
The order becomes a limit order at the stop price
The order is cancelled
The order becomes a market order and executes at the best available price
w: Wrong: because it becomes a market order, the fill can be above or below the stop price.
Wrong: a triggered stop order converts to a market order, not a limit order.
Wrong: reaching the stop price activates the order rather than cancelling it.
Correct: the stop price is only a trigger; once reached, the order converts to a market order and fills at the best available price.

questions.q: An investor bought 400 shares at $48 and the stock has risen to $55. She wants to protect part of her profit while staying invested. Which order should she enter?
o: Sell limit at $52
Sell stop at $52
Buy stop at $52
Buy limit at $52
w: Wrong: a sell limit at $52 sits below the current price and would be filled right away, not wait to protect against a drop.
Correct: a sell stop below the market protects a long position; if the price falls to $52 it becomes a market order and sells.
Wrong: a buy stop is used to protect a short position, not a long one.
Wrong: a buy limit would add to the position rather than protect the existing shares.

questions.q: A customer sold 300 shares of a stock short at $80 and wants to limit the potential loss if the price rises. Which order would accomplish this?
o: Sell stop at $86
Buy limit at $86
Sell limit at $86
Buy stop at $86
w: Wrong: a sell stop is for protecting a long position, not a short one.
Wrong: a buy limit at $86 sits above the market and would fill immediately, rather than waiting for the price to rise.
Wrong: a sell limit would add to the short position rather than close it.
Correct: a buy stop entered above the market triggers if the price rises to $86, becoming a market order that buys back the shares.

questions.q: A customer holds a sell stop for 400 shares at $45. The stock trades down to $45, triggering the order, but the best bid at that moment is $44.60. What are the gross proceeds of the sale?
w: Wrong: $17,800 corresponds to a price of $44.50, which is not the best available bid.
Wrong: $18,000 assumes execution exactly at the $45 stop price, which a stop order does not guarantee.
Correct: the triggered stop becomes a market order filled at the best bid, $44.60 × 400 = $17,840.
Wrong: $17,900 corresponds to $44.75, not the stated best bid of $44.60.

questions.q: Which pair of orders is entered below the current market price?
o: Buy limit and sell stop
Buy stop and sell stop
Buy stop and buy limit
Buy limit and sell limit
w: Correct: buy limit and sell stop are both entered below the market (BLiSS).
Wrong: the buy stop is above the market and only the sell stop is below it.
Wrong: the buy stop is entered above the market, so this pair is mixed.
Wrong: the sell limit is entered above the market, so the pair is split.

questions.q:
Which of the following orders are entered above the current market price?

I. Buy limit
II. Sell limit
III. Buy stop
IV. Sell stop
o: I and IV only
III and IV only
I and II only
II and III only
w: Wrong: buy limit and sell stop are the two orders entered below the market.
Wrong: buy stop is above the market but sell stop is below it.
Wrong: buy limit is below the market while sell limit is above, so the pair is split.
Correct: sell limit and buy stop are entered above the market (SLoBS).

questions.q: A customer has an open GTC order to buy 100 shares at a limit of $56. The stock goes ex-dividend with a $0.80 cash dividend. With no special instructions, what is the limit price after the ex-date?
w: Correct: buy limit orders are reduced by the dividend amount, so $56.00 − $0.80 = $55.20.
Wrong: a buy limit entered below the market is reduced on the ex-date, so it does not stay at $56.
Wrong: orders are only adjusted downward, never upward, so $56.80 is impossible.
Wrong: $55.00 subtracts $1.00 rather than the actual $0.80 dividend.

questions.q: A stock trades at $30. One customer holds a sell stop at $28.50 and another holds a buy stop at $32. The stock goes ex-dividend with a $0.45 dividend. After the ex-date, what are the order prices?
o: Sell stop $28.05; buy stop $31.55
Sell stop $28.05; buy stop $32.00
Sell stop $28.50; buy stop $32.00
Sell stop $28.95; buy stop $32.45
w: Wrong: the buy stop is above the market, so it is not reduced; only the sell stop is adjusted.
Correct: sell stop is a BLiSS order, so $28.50 − $0.45 = $28.05, while the buy stop is a SLoBS order and remains $32.00.
Wrong: the sell stop is entered below the market and is adjusted, so it does not stay at $28.50.
Wrong: orders adjust only downward, never up, so these higher prices cannot result.

questions.q: A stock closes at $71 the day before it goes ex-dividend with a $1.00 dividend, and opens at $70 on the ex-date. A customer holds a GTC buy limit at $70 with a do not reduce (DNR) instruction. What happens?
o: The limit is reduced to $69 and the order does not execute at the open
The limit is raised to $71 to match the prior close
The limit stays at $70 and the order can execute at the open
The order is cancelled on the ex-date
w: Wrong: reducing the limit to $69 is what would happen without DNR, but the instruction prevents that adjustment.
Wrong: orders are never adjusted upward, and DNR simply leaves the price unchanged.
Correct: DNR stops the reduction, so the limit remains $70 and, even if that causes execution at the open, it is allowed.
Wrong: ex-date does not cancel GTC orders; it only adjusts certain prices unless DNR is attached.

questions.q: A stock is offered at $25.00 on one trading venue and $25.08 on another. A broker-dealer buys it for a customer at $25.08 without any justification related to volatility or liquidity. Which statement is correct?
o: This is front-running
This satisfies best execution because both venues are legitimate
This is acceptable because it is a principal trade
This fails the best execution obligation
w: Wrong: front-running involves trading ahead of a block on non-public information, which is not described.
Wrong: legitimacy of the venue does not matter; the customer must receive the most advantageous terms available.
Wrong: best execution applies to both agency and principal trades.
Correct: best execution requires routing to the venue offering the most favorable terms, and paying more with no justification fails that duty.

questions.q: A broker-dealer sends a customer’s order through another broker-dealer acting as principal. The extra firm adds fees but provides no price improvement or other benefit to the customer. This practice is called:
o: interpositioning
backing away
order-splitting
spoofing
w: Correct: inserting an unnecessary additional principal broker-dealer with no customer benefit is interpositioning, a best-execution violation.
Wrong: backing away is failing to honor a firm quote.
Wrong: order-splitting means dividing one order into several small orders, not adding a firm to the chain.
Wrong: spoofing means entering orders without intent to execute in order to move prices.

questions.q: A firm handles a customer’s 2,000-share order. Which of the following practices would be permitted under FINRA’s order-splitting rule?
o: Dividing the order into twenty 100-share orders so it can charge twenty commissions
Dividing the order mainly to increase the firm’s total payments
Dividing the order into smaller pieces because the firm believes smaller orders will fill faster and at better prices
Dividing the order so that a related broker-dealer can act as principal on each piece
w: Wrong: splitting solely to collect more commissions is the classic prohibited trade-shredding.
Wrong: splitting with the primary purpose of increasing payments is prohibited by Rule 5290.
Correct: splitting for legitimate reasons such as obtaining better and faster execution is allowed.
Wrong: adding principal intermediaries with no benefit would be interpositioning and a fee-driven split.

questions.q: Under the rules described in the chapter, within what period must an equity trade be reported, and within what period must a municipal bond trade be reported to the MSRB’s RTRS (under the rule currently in force)?
o: 15 minutes; 10 seconds
10 seconds; 15 minutes
10 minutes; 15 seconds
60 seconds; 1 hour
w: Wrong: the two time periods are reversed between equities and municipals.
Correct: equity trades are reported within 10 seconds, and municipal trades within 15 minutes under MSRB Rule G-14.
Wrong: the units are swapped; equities are 10 seconds and munis are 15 minutes.
Wrong: neither period matches the required equity or municipal reporting times.

questions.q: FINRA prohibits firms from paying media outlets to influence the price of a security. Which of the following is NOT prohibited?
o: A clearly identified paid advertisement
Paying a newspaper columnist to write favorably about an issuer
Paying a radio host to promote a stock without disclosing the payment
Giving a publication anything of value in return for a bullish article
w: Correct: clearly identified paid advertising is an exception, along with research reports.
Wrong: paying a columnist to write favorably is an attempt to influence the price and is prohibited.
Wrong: an undisclosed payment to promote a stock is the type of manipulative payment the rule prohibits.
Wrong: giving anything of value for favorable coverage is covered by the prohibition.

questions.q: A registered representative learns that a large customer is about to place an order to buy 25,000 shares of a stock. Before the order is entered, he buys 200 shares for his own account. This is:
o: permitted because 200 shares is a small order
front-running, which is prohibited
an example of best execution
permitted because the customer’s order has not yet been executed
w: Wrong: the size of the personal order does not matter; trading ahead on knowledge of a block is prohibited.
Correct: trading on material nonpublic knowledge of an imminent block trade of 10,000 shares or more is front-running.
Wrong: best execution concerns routing a customer’s order to the best venue, not personal trading.
Wrong: the lack of execution is exactly why the rule bites; it applies before the block trade is executed and reported.

questions.q: A broker-dealer holds an unexecuted customer order to buy 3,000 shares of a stock at a limit of $18.50. The firm buys 1,000 shares for its own inventory at $18.50. What must the firm do to comply with FINRA’s rule on trading ahead of customer orders?
o: Nothing, since the customer’s limit has not yet been reached
Fill the customer’s entire 3,000 shares within 60 seconds
Fill the customer’s order for at least 1,000 shares at $18.50 or better within 60 seconds
Cancel the customer’s order and notify the customer within 10 seconds
w: Wrong: the firm traded at a price equal to the customer’s limit, which triggers the obligation.
Wrong: the requirement is at least the number of shares the firm bought for itself, not the whole order.
Correct: the firm must immediately, within 60 seconds, fill the customer at the same or better price for at least the number of shares it bought, here 1,000.
Wrong: cancelling is not the remedy; the firm must execute the customer’s order, and the clock is 60 seconds.

questions.q: A trader enters a large number of orders with no intention of executing them, to entice other participants to join one side of the market, and then trades against those participants. This is known as:
o: arbitrage
interpositioning
trade-shredding
spoofing
w: Wrong: arbitrage exploits a temporary price difference and is not manipulation.
Wrong: interpositioning is adding an unnecessary broker-dealer as principal to a customer trade.
Wrong: trade-shredding is splitting a customer order mainly to increase fees.
Correct: entering orders with no intent to execute to influence prices and then trading against others is spoofing.

questions.q: A firm’s research department is about to publish a favorable report on XYZ Corp. A trader at the same firm, who has heard about it, buys call options on XYZ for the firm’s own inventory before the report is released. Which statement is correct?
o: This is permitted because the trade is in options rather than in stock
This is acceptable if the trader tells the customers afterwards
This is permitted because the trade is for the firm’s own account
This violates the rule on trading ahead of research reports, which also covers derivatives
w: Wrong: the rule covers the security and derivatives of the issuer, such as call options.
Wrong: after-the-fact disclosure does not cure trading on nonpublic research information.
Wrong: the rule is aimed precisely at the firm trading from its own inventory.
Correct: establishing, increasing or decreasing inventory positions in a security or derivative ahead of a research report is prohibited under Rule 5280.

questions.q: An investor buys a stock on one exchange at a low price and immediately resells it on another exchange at a higher price. How is this activity treated?
o: Marking the close
Spoofing
Arbitrage, which is not considered manipulation
A pump and dump
w: Wrong: marking the close involves orders entered near the close to move the closing price, which did not occur.
Wrong: spoofing involves orders without intent to execute, but both trades here were real.
Correct: taking advantage of a temporary price disparity is arbitrage and is not manipulation.
Wrong: a pump and dump relies on exaggerated or misleading hype, which is absent.

questions.q: The CEO of an issuer offers a trader at a broker-dealer a generous gift of stock if the firm agrees to begin quoting and making a market in the issuer’s shares. What is the correct analysis?
o: It is permitted if the gift is disclosed to the firm’s principal
It is prohibited because a firm may not accept direct or indirect payment from an issuer, its affiliates or promoters for making a market
It is permitted if the stock is traded on the OTC Bulletin Board
It is permitted if the market maker quotes at least one round lot
w: Wrong: disclosure does not make an issuer payment for market making acceptable.
Correct: FINRA Rule 5250 bars direct or indirect payments, including securities, from issuers, affiliates or promoters in return for quoting or making a market.
Wrong: the venue does not change the rule against accepting such payments.
Wrong: quote size is irrelevant to the conflict of interest the rule prevents.

questions.q:
Which of the following are examples of prohibited market manipulation?

I. Marking the close
II. Pump and dump
III. Circulating false rumors about a security
IV. Arbitrage between two exchanges
o: I, II and III only
I and II only
II, III and IV only
I, II, III and IV
w: Correct: marking the close, pump and dump, and circulating rumors are all prohibited, while arbitrage is not manipulation.
Wrong: this leaves out circulating rumors, which the chapter also lists as prohibited manipulation.
Wrong: this wrongly includes arbitrage and omits marking the close.
Wrong: arbitrage takes advantage of a temporary price disparity and is not treated as manipulation.

questions.q: A trader at Firm A tells a trader at Firm B that if Firm B does not raise its quote in a stock, Firm A will stop sending it order flow. Which rule is implicated?
o: Best execution rules on interpositioning
The rule on trading ahead of research reports
The anti-coordination and anti-intimidation rule, which bars threatening another member to alter a price or quote
The requirement to report trades within 10 seconds
w: Wrong: interpositioning concerns adding an unnecessary broker-dealer to a customer trade.
Wrong: research-report rules concern trading ahead of published research, which is not involved.
Correct: FINRA Rule 5240 requires independent quoting and prohibits directing, requesting or threatening another member to change a price or quote.
Wrong: trade reporting deadlines are unrelated to pressuring another firm’s quotes.

questions.q: Which statement describes a DVP/RVP account?
o: An account that lets retail customers trade after hours on an ECN
A retail margin account that holds securities as loan collateral
A discretionary account managed by the representative
An institutional account used to settle trades by delivery or receipt versus payment, which does not hold securities positions
w: Wrong: ECNs serve subscribers such as broker-dealers and large institutions, and a DVP/RVP account is a settlement arrangement rather than an after-hours trading feature.
Wrong: holding securities as collateral for a loan is a margin feature, and a DVP/RVP account does not hold positions at all.
Wrong: discretion concerns who decides the trades, not how they settle, so it does not describe a DVP/RVP arrangement.
Correct: institutions sometimes clear trades through delivery-versus-payment or receipt-versus-payment accounts, and these accounts hold no securities positions.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares limit orders and stop orders?
o: Neither can ever be filled at a price better than the stated price
A limit order can be filled in part, while a triggered stop order is executed in full
Both are guaranteed to execute at their stated price
A triggered stop order can be filled in part, while a limit order is always filled in full
w: Wrong: a limit order is filled at the limit price or better, so a better price is entirely possible.
Correct: a limit order may be only partly filled if the price is not available for every share, whereas a stop order, once triggered, becomes a market order and is fully executed.
Wrong: a limit order guarantees a price but not execution, and a stop order guarantees neither price nor a fill at the stop level.
Wrong: this reverses the two; a limit order may go unfilled in whole or in part, while a triggered stop executes completely.

questions.q: All of the following are services that an exchange provides to the market EXCEPT:
o: guaranteeing payment to the seller and delivering shares to the buyer
giving issuers and investors liquidity
automatically reporting transaction data
deciding which stocks an individual investor should buy
w: Wrong: exchanges act as clearinghouses, guaranteeing payment to the seller and delivering the purchased shares to the buyer, so this is a service they provide.
Wrong: providing liquidity, the ability to sell quickly and easily, is a core service of an exchange.
Wrong: exchanges automatically report transaction data to the appropriate reporting facility.
Correct: choosing what to buy is an investment decision for the investor and adviser, not a service an exchange performs.

questions.q: For regular-way trades, how does the ex-dividend date relate to the record date?
o: It is one business day after the record date
It is the same day as the record date
It is two business days before the record date
It is the payable date
w: Wrong: the stock does not go ex a day after the record date; by then ownership on the record has already been settled.
Correct: for regular-way trades the ex-dividend date falls on the same day as the record date.
Wrong: an ex-date two business days ahead of the record date describes an older settlement cycle, not the relationship tested here.
Wrong: the payable date is when the dividend is paid, which comes after the ex-date.

questions.q: A customer wants to buy 100 shares of a large, heavily traded stock right now and cares far more about speed than about a few cents of price. Which order fits best?
o: Sell stop order
Buy limit order well below the market
Good ’til cancelled buy limit order
Market order
w: Wrong: a sell stop is a sell-side protective order, and this customer is buying.
Wrong: a buy limit far below the market may sit unfilled, so it does not deliver the speed the customer wants.
Wrong: a GTC limit order stays open until filled or cancelled but cannot promise a prompt execution.
Correct: a market order gives immediate execution at the best available price, which suits a small trade in a liquid stock when speed matters most.

questions.q: Which condition is needed for a broker-dealer to execute a trade as agent?
o: The firm must be the registered market maker in the security
The firm must first buy the shares for its own inventory
Two other market participants willing to transact on the same terms at the same time
The customer must pay a mark-up instead of a commission
w: Wrong: market-maker status is not required for matching two customers as agent.
Wrong: buying into inventory is what a dealer does in a principal trade, and an agent never owns the security.
Correct: an agency trade needs a willing buyer and a willing seller, other than the firm, on agreeable terms at the same time.
Wrong: a mark-up belongs to principal trades, while agency trades are paid by commission.
